It is held in para No.19 is as under;

In the background of the factual and legal position taken note supra, in the instant facts, the appellant cannot be nonsuited for proceeding with the complaint filed under Section 138 of N.I.Act merely due to the fact that SCCH10 the cheques presented and dishounoured are shown to have been issued as security, as indicated in the loan agreement.

In the aforesaid back drop, though the accused has taken the contention that the cheque was issued for security purpose, it is apparent that on the date of presentation of the cheque the accused was liable to pay huge amount to the complainant towards the loan due from him.

sentences.text: It is not in dispute that, the complainant has filed the present complaint against the accused for the commission of offence punishable u/s 138 of N.I.Act and also initiated arbitral proceedings.

It is settled principles of law that, the proceedings u/s 138 of N.I.Act and the arbitral proceedings are distinct one and the arbitration is a remedy for seeking the relief for breaching of an agreement.
The proceedings u/s 138 is a penal proceedings for the commission of offence by the accused for dishonour of cheque.
The SCCH10 Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Trisuns Chemical Industry Vs Rajesh Agarawal and ors.

entities.text: Trisuns Chemical Industry Vs Rajesh Agarawal and ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: held that, "merely because arbitration proceedings have been under taken, the criminal proceedings could not be thwarted".
23. It is needles to state that even if the arbitral award amount is recovered, that can be adjusted towards compensation were to be ordered by this Court.

In the instant case, though the complainant has initiated arbitral proceedings against the accused, but the said procedure is obviously civil in nature and the present proceeding is criminal in nature to penalize the accused.
Therefore, the argument canvassed by the learned counsel for the accused cannot be accepted.

24. Even though the PW1 was crossexamined in length by the counsel for the accused, except mere suggestions SCCH10 and denials nothing was elicited from the mouth of PW1 to support the contention of the defence.
25. Under the criminal jurisprudence, prosecution is required to establish the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt.
However, the proceeding u/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act is quasi criminal in nature.
In these proceedings proof beyond reasonable doubt is subject to presumptions envisaged Under Secs.118, 139 and 146 of Negotiable Instrument Act.

An offence under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act is committed not on dishonour of cheque, but on failure of drawer of the cheque to make repayment within 15 days of the receipt of notice of dishonour.
An essential ingredients of Sec.138 of Negotiable Instrument Act is that cheque in question must have been issued towards a legally enforceable debt or liability.
Secs.118 and 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act envisage certain presumptions.
Under Sec.118, a presumption shall be raised regarding consideration, date, SCCH10 transfer, endorsement and regarding the holder in case of Negotiable Instruments.
Even under Sec.139 a rebuttable presumption shall be raised that the cheque in question was issued regarding discharge of a legally enforceable debt.
These presumptions are mandatory presumptions that are required to be raised in case of Negotiable Instruments.
These presumptions are not conclusive presumptions, but are rebuttable.
As these presumptions are mandated by the law they are to be raised in every case affecting Negotiable Instruments.

This position of law has been highlighted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decisions reported in 2001 Crl.L.J. 4647 (S.C.) between:
Hiten P.Dalal V/s Bratindranath Banerjee, 2001(8) SCC 458 between: K.N.Beena Vs.
Muniyappan & Another and in AIR 2010 S.C. 1898 between Rangappa V/s Mohan.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 26. Such being the case it is for the accused to rebut the presumption under Sec.139 of Negotiable Instruments Act SCCH10 and to show that the cheque in question was not issued towards any legally enforceable debt or liability and accused has to prove the same not by mere plausible explanation, but by cogent evidence.

sentences.text:
As it has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decision reported in 2008(1) Crimes 227 (SC) between:
Krishna Janardhan Bhat Vs. Dattatraya G.Hegde that :
(a) Negotiable Instrument Act 1881 - Sec.118(b) - The Courts below committed a serious error in proceeding on the basis that for proving the defence the accused is required to step into the witness box, and unless he does so he would not be discharging his burden.
(c) Indian Evidence Act, 1872 - Sec.101 - Burden of proof - Whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of an accused is SCCH10 'preponderance of probabilities' - Such inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on records by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies.

entities.text: Krishna Janardhan Bhat Vs. Dattatraya G.Hegde
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the above said respected judgment it is held that accused need not step into the witness box to prove his defence and the standard of proof is to prove the defence on part of an accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'.
Such preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties, but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies.

28. In the present case, though the accused has defended that the cheque in question was issued towards security and not for repayment of any legally enforceable debt, the accused has neither produced any materials to show that the said cheque was issued for security.
The accused at the time of crossexamination, suggested to PW1 that the SCCH10 cheque was issued for security purpose.
But Pw1 has categorically denied the same.
Mere suggestions and denial will not serve any purpose and it will not shift the burden of the accused.
In the instant case, the accused has not denied the transaction between the complainant and himself.
Accused has also admitted the issuance of cheque to the complainant.
Further, the accused has not denied his signature in Ex.P1 cheque.
As such the complainant has proved his initial burden.
But the accused has not produced any cogent evidence to disprove the contention of the complainant.
In the present case, the materials placed by the complainant are much probable than that of the defence taken by the accused.
The oral evidence of PW1 coupled with Ex.P.1 to Ex.P.22 corroborates with each other.
29. The complaint was presented within a prescribed period of limitation.
The complainant has also complied the mandatory provisions as required u/sec. 138 of N.I. Act.
SCCH10

On appreciation of oral and documentary evidence on record, it is crystal clear that, the accused has issued Ex.P.1 cheque in discharge of legally enforceable debt and the accused has failed to repay the amount and thereby committed an offence punishable u/sec.138 of N.I. Act.
Accordingly, I answer Point No.1 in the affirmative.

sentences.text: POINT NO.2:
In view of the reasons stated and discussed above, the complainant has proved that the accused has committed an offence punishable under Section 138 of N.I. Act.

Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in a decision reported in, (2015) 17 SCC 368, in a case of H.Pukhraj Vs. D.Parasmal, observed that, having regard to the length of trial and date of issuance of the cheque, it is necessary to award reasonable interest on the cheque amount along with cost of litigation.

Further the Hon'ble Apex Court in its recent decision in M/s. Meters & instrument Pvt Ltd. Vs. SCCH10 Kanchana Mehta reported in (2018)1 SCC560 held at para 18 that "The object of the provision being primarily compensatory, punitive element being mainly with the object of enforcing the compensatory element, compounding at the initial stage has to be encouraged but is not debarred at later stage subject to appropriate compensation as may be found acceptable to the parties or the Court."

entities.text: M/s. Meters & instrument Pvt Ltd. Vs. SCCH10 Kanchana Mehta reported in (2018)1 SCC560
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
31. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the judgment of Mainuddin Abdul Sattar Shaikh Vs Vijay.D Salvi reported in (2015) 9 SCC 622 held that, "as the provision of chapter XVII of the Act strongly lean towards grant of reimbursement of the loss by way of compensation, the Courts should unless there are special circumstance, in all cases of conviction, uniformly exercise the power to levy fine up to twice the cheque amount (keeping in view the cheque amount and the simple interest thereon at 9%
per SCCH10 annum as the reasonable quantum of loss) and direct payment of such amount as compensation.

entities.text: Mainuddin Abdul Sattar Shaikh Vs Vijay.D Salvi reported in (2015) 9 SCC 622
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, keeping in mind the time when the transaction has taken place and primary object of the provision, this Court is of the opinion that, rather than imposing punitive sentence, if sentence of fine is imposed with a direction to compensate the complainant for his monitory loss, by awarding compensation U/Sec.357 of Cr.P.C, would meet the ends of justice.
By keeping in mind Sec.143(1), Sec.80 and 117 of the Act, the compensation has to be awarded.
As per the records, the transaction was taken place in the year 2019 and the cheque was dated 10.08.2020 and amount covered under said cheque is Rs.41,10,000/.
It appears that, the complainant has spent considerable time and money to prosecute the case.

By considering all these aspects, this Court is of the opinion that, it is just and proper to impose fine amount of Rs.45,00,000/, which includes interest and cost of litigation, out of which compensation of SCCH10 Rs.44,90,000/ has to be awarded to the complainant.

Accordingly, this Court proceeds to pass the following;
ORDER Acting under Section 255(2) of Cr.P.C., the accused is found guilty and he is convicted for the offence punishable under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act and he is sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.45,00,000/ (Rupees Forty Five Lakhs only).
In default to pay the fine, accused shall undergo simple imprisonment for a period of six months.

Further, acting under Sec.357(1)(b) of Cr.P.C., a sum of Rs.44,90,000/ (Rupees Forty Four lakhs and Ninety thousand only) on recovery shall be paid to the complainant as compensation and Rs.10,000/ shall be remitted SCCH10 to the state exchequer for the expenses incurred for prosecution.

An offence under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act is committed not on dishonour of cheque, but on failure of drawer of the cheque to make repayment within 15 days of the receipt of notice of dishonour.
An essential ingredients of Sec.138 of Negotiable Instrument Act is that cheque in question must have been issued towards a legally enforceable debt or liability.
Secs.118 and 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act envisage certain presumptions.
Under Sec.118, a presumption shall be raised regarding consideration, date, SCCH10 transfer, endorsement and regarding the holder in case of Negotiable Instruments.
Even under Sec.139 a rebuttable presumption shall be raised that the cheque in question was issued regarding discharge of a legally enforceable debt.
These presumptions are mandatory presumptions that are required to be raised in case of Negotiable Instruments.
These presumptions are not conclusive presumptions, but are rebuttable.
As these presumptions are mandated by the law they are to be raised in every case affecting Negotiable Instruments.
Such preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties, but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies.
Mere suggestions and denial will not serve any purpose and it will not shift the burden of the accused.
In the instant case, the accused has not denied the transaction between the complainant and himself.
As such the complainant has proved his initial burden.
But the accused has not produced any cogent evidence to disprove the contention of the complainant.
In the present case, the materials placed by the complainant are much probable than that of the defence taken by the accused.
The oral evidence of PW1 coupled with Ex.P.1 to Ex.P.22 corroborates with each other.
